evidence.claim: Kishida tied his economic agenda to wage increases, tax incentives for wage hikes, help for SMEs to pass through higher costs, a minimum wage above 1,000 yen, and greater investment in people.
evidence.title: Policy Speech by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio to the 208th Session of the Diet
evidence.excerpt: Kishida tied his economic agenda to wage increases, tax incentives for wage hikes, help for SMEs to pass through higher costs, a minimum wage above 1,000 yen, and greater investment in people.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary official policy speech by the ruler, dated and explicit about intended economic policy choices.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct: Kishida set the agenda and asked the government to implement it; execution still depended on ministries, firms, and labor-market bargaining.
contrary_evidence: Later inflation and weak yen reduced real purchasing power, so intent did not automatically translate into household gains.

evidence.claim: After the August 2022 reshuffle, Kishida reappointed Shunichi Suzuki as finance minister and tasked him with overseeing exchange-rate fluctuations while balancing growth spending with fiscal reform.
evidence.title: Factbox-Profiles of Japanese cabinet ministers after Kishida reshuffle
evidence.excerpt: After the August 2022 reshuffle, Kishida reappointed Shunichi Suzuki as finance minister and tasked him with overseeing exchange-rate fluctuations while balancing growth spending with fiscal reform.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting is strong independent coverage, though the page is republished on Investing.com and the competence inference remains partial.
evidence.period_fit: Target-period contemporaneous coverage of a 2022 cabinet reshuffle.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct appointment by Kishida; competence is inferred from portfolio assignment and prior experience, not proven by the article alone.
contrary_evidence: The same report notes Suzuki is closely aligned with the finance ministry line, so this does not prove policy innovation or success.
Political retention of veterans can reflect continuity as much as merit.

evidence.claim: Suzuki said Japan would pursue a new capitalism and a 2022 budget/tax package while also keeping the 2025 primary-balance surplus goal and broader fiscal consolidation in view.
evidence.title: 第208回国会における鈴木財務大臣の財政演説
evidence.excerpt: Suzuki said Japan would pursue a new capitalism and a 2022 budget/tax package while also keeping the 2025 primary-balance surplus goal and broader fiscal consolidation in view.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary fiscal-policy speech by the finance minister, with explicit budget and fiscal-management commitments.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect but relevant: the finance minister articulated the fiscal posture of Kishida's cabinet; the policy line was part of Kishida's administration, not Kishida alone.
contrary_evidence: The budget remained highly expansionary and Japan still carried very high public debt.
This is an aspiration and policy frame, not proof of durable fiscal correction.

evidence.claim: The IMF said Japan was recovering under strong policy support but still needed deep reforms to raise productivity and achieve inclusive, sustainable growth; it projected 2022 real GDP growth of 2.4 percent and headline inflation of 1.0 percent.
evidence.title: Japan: 2022 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Japan
evidence.excerpt: The IMF said Japan was recovering under strong policy support but still needed deep reforms to raise productivity and achieve inclusive, sustainable growth; it projected 2022 real GDP growth of 2.4 percent and headline inflation of 1.0 percent.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Authoritative multilateral surveillance, but the full report page was partly blocked in browsing and this claim is drawn from the accessible report snippet and table excerpt.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly contextual: reflects inherited macro conditions and cabinet policy support rather than a single Kishida action.
contrary_evidence: These are projections, not end-of-year outcomes.
The same report emphasizes structural reforms Kishida had not yet completed.

evidence.claim: The OECD table shows 2022 GDP growth at 1.0 percent, gross public debt at 244.8 percent of GDP, and headline inflation at 2.5 percent.
evidence.title: Executive Summary: OECD Economic Surveys: Japan 2024
evidence.excerpt: The OECD table shows 2022 GDP growth at 1.0 percent, gross public debt at 244.8 percent of GDP, and headline inflation at 2.5 percent.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official OECD country-survey table with retrospective 2022 outcomes and clear numeric indicators.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect: the numbers reflect the inherited macro baseline, global shocks, and cabinet policy response rather than a single fully attributable decision.
contrary_evidence: The debt level remained extremely high, and inflation was above the BOJ target.
The data do not isolate Kishida's marginal contribution.

evidence.claim: For 2022, workers' household monthly income rose 2.0 percent nominally but fell 1.0 percent in real terms, while monthly consumption also lagged inflation in real terms.
evidence.title: News Bulletin February 28, 2023
evidence.excerpt: For 2022, workers' household monthly income rose 2.0 percent nominally but fell 1.0 percent in real terms, while monthly consumption also lagged inflation in real terms.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official statistical bulletin with directly reported household-income and spending figures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Contextual and partly attributable: it reflects the inflation shock Kishida was trying to offset, but not his control over every household outcome.
contrary_evidence: Nominal income did rise, so the squeeze was real but not uniformly negative in cash terms.
This does not isolate effects by region or gender.

evidence.claim: The labor ministry said 2022 real wages fell because inflation's negative effect outweighed nominal wage gains, even though spring wage settlements rose 2.20 percent and most firms raised wages.
evidence.title: 第Ⅰ部　第３章　労働時間・賃金等の動向｜令和５年版　労働経済の分析
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, Japan
evidence.excerpt: The labor ministry said 2022 real wages fell because inflation's negative effect outweighed nominal wage gains, even though spring wage settlements rose 2.20 percent and most firms raised wages.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official labor ministry analysis with direct wage, wage-settlement, and inflation-adjustment discussion.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective analysis of 2022 labor and wage outcomes.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partial: Kishida pushed a wage-growth agenda, but real-wage outcomes were also driven by imported inflation and employer bargaining.
contrary_evidence: Nominal wage settlements improved relative to 2021, so the cabinet's wage push was not ineffective in nominal terms.
The report does not measure the fiscal cost or durability of the policy mix.

evidence.claim: The OECD estimated that household purchasing power fell 3 percent in Japan between August 2021 and August 2022, with low-income and rural households hit especially hard.
evidence.title: A cost-of-living squeeze? Distributional implications of rising inflation
evidence.excerpt: The OECD estimated that household purchasing power fell 3 percent in Japan between August 2021 and August 2022, with low-income and rural households hit especially hard.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: OECD analysis directly quantifies household welfare effects and distributional incidence from inflation.
evidence.period_fit: Very close to the 2022 target period and explicitly measures 2021-2022 purchasing-power change.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect but important: it captures the cost-of-living shock Kishida responded to, not a solely ruler-created outcome.
contrary_evidence: This is a cross-country distributional analysis, not a pure Kishida performance audit.
It captures the burden side better than the remedy side.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Japan unveiled a $200 billion stimulus package to tame inflation, including subsidies to cut household electricity bills 20 percent and an extension of gasoline subsidies, with the government saying the package would cut consumer prices by about 1.2 percentage points.
evidence.title: Japan unveils $200 billion in new spending to ease inflation pain
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Japan unveiled a $200 billion stimulus package to tame inflation, including subsidies to cut household electricity bills 20 percent and an extension of gasoline subsidies, with the government saying the package would cut consumer prices by about 1.2 percentage points.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters is strong independent contemporaneous reporting with direct quotations from Kishida and budget details.
evidence.period_fit: Contemporaneous October 2022 action on inflation and energy prices.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct: Kishida publicly owned the package, but its effects depended on implementation and the BOJ's separate monetary stance.
contrary_evidence: The report notes concerns about debt, yen weakness, and policy mix risks.
The package relied heavily on subsidies, which may be temporary rather than structural.

evidence.claim: Kishida said the cabinet approved a 72-trillion-yen package to address rising prices and economic revival, lower electricity fees by 20 percent, cap gasoline prices, and boost GDP by 4.6 percent through 2023.
evidence.title: Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said the cabinet approved a 72-trillion-yen package to address rising prices and economic revival, lower electricity fees by 20 percent, cap gasoline prices, and boost GDP by 4.6 percent through 2023.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary official press conference with explicit policy commitments and quantitative targets.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct: Kishida announced and defended the package; execution still depended on the cabinet, parliament, and firms/households.
contrary_evidence: The package is heavily stimulus-oriented and therefore raises fiscal-sustainability questions.
The promised GDP and price effects were targets, not verified outcomes at the time.

evidence.claim: The Kishida Cabinet's New Form of Capitalism page says structural wage growth should come through reskilling, job-based pay, labor mobility into growth fields, and a larger middle class, alongside public-private investment, startups, GX, DX, and AI governance.
evidence.title: A New Form of Capitalism
evidence.excerpt: The Kishida Cabinet's New Form of Capitalism page says structural wage growth should come through reskilling, job-based pay, labor mobility into growth fields, and a larger middle class, alongside public-private investment, startups, GX, DX, and AI governance.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary policy page from the PMO describing the cabinet's economic strategy in Kishida's own terms.
evidence.period_fit: Policy framing active during 2022 and carried through the period.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct in intent and agenda-setting; implementation depended on ministries, firms, and regulatory follow-through.
contrary_evidence: The page is aspirational and does not itself prove implementation or distributional success.
Some proposals, such as asset-income expansion and investment-led growth, may benefit capital owners more than low-income households unless paired with effective redistribution.

evidence.claim: Suzuki said the second FY2022 supplementary budget would appropriate about 28.92 trillion yen, including 7.82 trillion yen for price hikes and wage increases and 3.49 trillion yen for regional earning power, while promoting responsible economic and fiscal management.
evidence.title: Speech on Fiscal Policy by Minister of Finance Suzuki at the 210th Session of the National Diet
evidence.excerpt: Suzuki said the second FY2022 supplementary budget would appropriate about 28.92 trillion yen, including 7.82 trillion yen for price hikes and wage increases and 3.49 trillion yen for regional earning power, while promoting responsible economic and fiscal management.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary finance-ministry speech with exact budget amounts and policy rationale.
evidence.period_fit: Direct late-2022 budget action for the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect but material: the finance minister spoke for Kishida's cabinet and implemented its fiscal posture.
contrary_evidence: The supplementary budget increased spending substantially, which cuts against a strict fiscal-restraint reading.
Fiscal support can cushion inflation but also add to Japan's already high debt.

unresolved_gaps: Direct cabinet-level records on Kishida's private command-and-control choices around safeguards, emergency procedures, and technical nuclear governance are thin.
Direct evidence of behind-the-scenes mediation, ceasefire brokerage, or proxy-control choices is thin.
The dossier remains thin on a ruler-specific pre-July 2022 domestic protection record, so most of the strong evidence is reactive to the Abe assassination and the Unification Church fallout.
Direct evidence of court, media, or election-administration capture attempts by Kishida is thin; most negative evidence is baseline openness plus remedial scandal cleanup.
Direct anti-capture, procurement, or favoritism evidence is thin relative to the amount of policy and macroeconomic material.
Subgroup-specific uptake and outcome evidence for poverty, disability, migrants, and regional disparities remains thin.
The dossier lacks direct 2022 evidence on Kishida's own assets, gifts, campaign finance, hidden conflicts, or family enrichment.
Independent evaluation of New Capitalism implementation and the causal contribution of Kishida's team remains limited; several follow-up items are government self-assessments or macro context.
